title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
openingText: In a village in La Mancha — the name of which I'd rather not recall — there lived not long ago one of those gentlemen who keep a lance in the rack, an old shield, a lean hack, and a greyhound for hunting. A stew of rather more beef than mutton, a salad most nights, leftovers on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays, and an extra pigeon on Sundays ate up three-quarters of his income.
about:
Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605, when he was fifty-seven, a wounded veteran of Lepanto, a former captive of Algerian pirates, and a failed tax collector who had spent time in debtors' prison. The book was a sensation across Europe within months. He published a second part in 1615, partly to displace a forged sequel by a writer using the pseudonym Avellaneda, and died the following year. The two parts together are usually counted as the first modern novel.

The story is simple in outline. An ageing country gentleman in La Mancha reads so many chivalric romances that his wits give way; he names himself Don Quixote, drafts a neighbouring peasant named Sancho Panza as his squire, declares a farmer's daughter named Aldonza Lorenzo to be the noble lady Dulcinea del Toboso, and rides out to revive the lost age of knight-errantry. Across 126 chapters he attacks windmills he believes are giants, mistakes inns for castles, and is beaten more often than he wins. In Part Two, written ten years later, everyone he meets has read Part One, knows who he is, and arranges elaborate practical jokes around him. He finally returns home, recovers his sanity, declares himself Alonso Quixano the Good, and dies. The novel's comedy and grief are inseparable: Cervantes invented a hero so vivid and so wrong that we have not yet finished reading him.

angleCards.title: The mad knight and what he sees.
angleCards.text: Don Quixote charges windmills he insists are giants, attacks a flock of sheep he insists is an enemy army, and sees in a country inn the high walls of an enchanted castle. The first question the book asks is not whether he is right but what his conviction is doing — how it shapes the people around him and what it costs him.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Don Quixote's perception of the world chapter by chapter and decide whether his madness is closer to delusion, performance, or a kind of vision the rest of the cast lacks.

angleCards.title: Sancho Panza's voice.
angleCards.text: Sancho arrives in Chapter 7 as a plain villager bribed with the promise of an island to govern. He stays beside Don Quixote across both parts, butchering proverbs, eating whenever he can, switching between obedience and shrewd resistance, and slowly becoming the moral counterweight to his master.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track how Sancho's voice changes as the book goes on, where his folk wisdom shows up sharper than Don Quixote's chivalric speech, and what the friendship between the two of them becomes by the end.

angleCards.title: Dulcinea and the loved ideal.
angleCards.text: Dulcinea del Toboso never appears in the novel. She is a peasant girl named Aldonza Lorenzo whom Don Quixote has elevated into a noble lady so that his knighthood will have an object to serve. Every adventure is undertaken in her name; every defeated enemy is sent to bow before her.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to watch what Don Quixote does with the figure of Dulcinea across both parts — how he defends her, how Sancho complicates her, what happens when Part Two confronts him with the real Aldonza — and decide what the book is saying about devotion to an ideal.

angleCards.title: Part Two: a book that knows it was a book.
angleCards.text: Part Two opens in 1615, ten years after Part One was published. Inside the fiction, almost everyone Don Quixote meets has already read Part One. Dukes stage elaborate jokes around him because they recognise him as a character. A forged sequel by Avellaneda has appeared, and Cervantes works it into the plot. The book turns into a strange double — a novel about a man who has become famous for the novel he is in.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to watch how the meta-fictional move in Part Two changes the comedy and the sadness of the book, and what it means for a character to live inside a story that has already been read.

cast.name: Don Quixote of La Mancha
cast.description: An ageing hidalgo named Alonso Quixano who has read so many chivalric romances that he believes himself the last knight-errant of the world. He furnishes himself with rusty armour and a starved horse, gives himself a new name, swears himself to a lady he has invented, and rides out to right wrongs that no longer exist. He is courteous, learned, brave in his way, and almost always wrong about what is in front of him. The whole novel turns on whether his madness is a private failure or a kind of clarity the world has lost.

cast.name: Sancho Panza
cast.description: A peasant from Don Quixote's village whom the knight recruits in Chapter 7 with the promise of an island to govern after their conquests. Plain, hungry, loyal, and rich in proverbs that he often mangles, Sancho rides beside Don Quixote across both parts on a donkey he calls Dapple. He believes and disbelieves his master in alternating measures. By the end of Part Two he is one of the most fully rendered ordinary people in Western literature, and the friendship between him and Don Quixote has become the book's emotional centre.

cast.name: Dulcinea del Toboso
cast.description: A peasant girl from the nearby village of El Toboso named Aldonza Lorenzo, whom Don Quixote has silently elevated into a noble lady and the object of his knightly devotion. Dulcinea never appears in the novel; she does not speak, has no scene, and may not know Don Quixote exists. Every adventure he undertakes is dedicated to her, and every enemy he defeats is dispatched to El Toboso to kneel before her. The gap between the Dulcinea he serves and the Aldonza who would answer the door is one of the book's permanent ironies.

cast.name: Rocinante
cast.description: Don Quixote's mount: a thin, broken-down hack of his own that he spends four days renaming in Chapter 1, finally settling on Rocinante — meaning, he tells himself, the foremost of all the rocines of the world. Rocinante can barely trot. He is wholly serious about his role. Cervantes treats him as a character throughout: he stumbles, falls, refuses obstacles, mourns when Don Quixote is wounded, and finally returns home with the knight to die soon after his master. He is the perfect emblem of the chivalric fantasy he has been pressed into carrying.

cast.name: Cide Hamete Benengeli
cast.description: An invented Moorish historian whom Cervantes claims to be merely translating. The conceit is announced in Chapter 9 of Part One, when the narrator says he found the manuscript by accident in a Toledo market and had it rendered out of Arabic. From that point on, the novel is supposedly Cide Hamete's chronicle, full of asides about his reliability and the difficulty of writing about so famous a knight. The device frees Cervantes to play with truth, source, translation, and reader trust — a meta-fictional move that the novel has been re-inventing for four centuries since.

cast.name: Sansón Carrasco
cast.description: A bachelor of arts newly returned from the University of Salamanca who appears in Part Two. Once he reads Part One and meets Don Quixote in person, he becomes the principal agent of a plan to bring the old knight home: he disguises himself first as the Knight of the Mirrors and later as the Knight of the White Moon, challenges Don Quixote to single combat, and eventually defeats him on a beach near Barcelona, on the condition that the loser will return to his village and lay down his arms for a year. Sansón is the most modern figure in the novel — a literary man using fiction to manage someone else's life.

acclaim.quote: It can be said that all prose fiction is a variation on the theme of Don Quixote.
acclaim.source: Lionel Trilling, "Manners, Morals, and the Novel" (1947), collected in The Liberal Imagination (1950)
acclaim.context: Trilling's essay locates the European and American novel's central preoccupation — the conflict between appearance and reality — in Cervantes's founding example.

acclaim.quote: With Cervantes the modern era opens; in his novel, Don Quixote setting forth into a world he could not recognise, the world appeared in its terrible ambiguity, the single divine Truth decomposed into myriad relative truths parcelled out by men.
acclaim.source: Milan Kundera, The Art of the Novel (1986), opening essay "The Depreciated Legacy of Cervantes"
acclaim.context: Kundera opens his book on the novel by arguing that the form itself — its relativising, sceptical, perspectival intelligence — begins with Don Quixote's first ride out of La Mancha.

whyItMatters.title: The First Modern Novel
whyItMatters.body: Don Quixote is the book the novel begins from. Cervantes set down a form that has been the dominant prose vehicle in Europe and the Americas ever since: a long, multi-stranded narrative built around a central character whose inner life is in conflict with the world he moves through, told by a self-aware narrator who can step back and ironise the story he is telling. He invented the side-plot interpolation, the unreliable source, the embedded forgery, the meta-fictional cameo, and the unromantic comic squire. Fielding, Sterne, Flaubert, Dickens, Tolstoy, Joyce, García Márquez, Bolaño — every novelist who has tried to write a long book about ordinary people in their own time has reached, knowingly or not, for instruments Cervantes assembled in 1605. The novel as a form is one of the great inventions of the early modern period, and it begins here.

whyItMatters.title: What Reading Does to the Reader
whyItMatters.body: Don Quixote goes mad from reading. The premise of Chapter 1 is that the hidalgo's library of chivalric romances has worked on him until he cannot distinguish their world from his own — and the rest of the book is the very long sequel to that diagnosis. Cervantes is not condemning reading; he is taking it seriously as something that reshapes perception, identity, and the way a person walks through a village. The Curate and the Barber's auto-da-fé of the library in Chapter 6 is famously playful — they argue over which volumes deserve burning and which deserve saving — and the joke is that nobody quite knows. Four centuries on, the question of what the texts and screens we steep ourselves in are doing to us, and whether the trade is a good one, is still the modern question.

whyItMatters.title: The Idealist and the Pragmatist as a Pair
whyItMatters.body: The deepest invention in the book is the pairing of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza. One is an ageing intellectual with a vision of the world that does not fit it; the other is a peasant whose grasp of how the world actually works is the book's truest realism. They argue with each other across nearly a thousand pages, and in the arguing each one slowly becomes inflected by the other — Sancho begins to speak as if some of the chivalric vocabulary applies to his own life, and Don Quixote begins to notice the world Sancho describes. The pairing is the template for every double act in fiction since, and every workplace, marriage, and political coalition that runs on the tension between someone who wants to remake the world and someone who has to live in it tomorrow.
